strengths: First formal guarantee on cost-adjusted simple regret for adaptive stopping in Bayesian optimization, establishing a theoretical foundation previously lacking in the field
Principled derivation of stopping rule from Pandora's Box theory with elegant connection between PBGI and LogEIPC through equivalence of stopping criteria (Equations 6, 9, 10)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across synthetic (1D/8D Bayesian regret) and empirical benchmarks (LCBench, NATS-Bench) with multiple cost types and scenarios
Careful attention to practical implementation details including stabilization periods, debouncing strategies, and handling of unknown costs via GP modeling
Well-executed experiments with proper statistical rigor (50 seeds, error bars, multiple cost-scaling factors, model mismatch analysis)
Clear presentation with effective motivation and illustrations of the cost-sensitivity of the stopping rule
weaknesses: Theorem 2's guarantee is weak, bounding cost-adjusted regret only by the 'Immediate' baseline (stop after first evaluation), which most BO algorithms should trivially exceed; no convergence rate or problem-dependent characterization provided

Theory for independent case (Weitzman 1979) does not directly transfer to correlated GP setting; only 'better-than-immediate' property is proven rather than true optimality for the practical correlated regime

Limited novelty in core stopping criterion, which derives from existing theory (Weitzman 1979, Gergatsouli & Tzamos 2023); main contribution is equivalence between PBGI/LogEIPC, shown through algebraic manipulation

Inconsistent empirical performance: method ranks 3rd or worse on NATS-Bench datasets (cifar100, ImageNet16-120, Figures 16-17), contradicting claims of consistently matching or outperforming other methods
Significant performance degradation under objective model mismatch, common in practice, with limited analysis of failure modes or proposed remedies beyond empirical observation

Problem-dependent hyperparameter λ requires practitioners to specify cost-objective trade-off (Section 3.2); Corollary 3's suggested λ = U/(B-C) acknowledged as potentially overly conservative, requiring fallback to PBGI-D heuristic
Implementation requires heuristic adjustments (stabilization period, debounce threshold ~20 iterations, moving average smoothing, Section 3.2) not covered by theory, creating theory-practice gap
Choice of post-update stopping (α_t^PBGI) over pre-update (α_{t-1}^PBGI) lacks theoretical justification; justified only by empirical comparison in Section D.2

strengths: Elegant theoretical contribution: natural derivation from Pandora's Box theory with novel connection between PBGI and LogEIPC stopping criteria (Theorem 2 appears to be first formal guarantee on cost-adjusted regret for adaptive stopping in BO)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple experiment types (1D/8D Bayesian regret, LCBench, NATS-Bench), 7+ baselines, multiple cost structures, hindsight baselines, 50 random seeds, excellent reproducibility details
Well-motivated practical problem: addresses genuine challenge in applications like cloud-based hyperparameter tuning where evaluation costs and solution quality both matter
Thoughtful methodological design: principled choice to use α^PBGI_t (after posterior update), well-justified design decisions, practical implementation guidance for deployment
Honest treatment of limitations: openly acknowledges performance degradation under model mismatch rather than overselling results
weaknesses: Weak theoretical guarantee: Theorem 2 only bounds cost-adjusted regret by the immediate baseline (stop after first evaluation), providing minimal assurance; no sublinear bounds or dependence on problem structure; limited practical value as guarantee

Significant theory-practice gap: theory assumes constant mean μ for f and noiseless evaluation; practice violates these assumptions; PBGI loses optimality guarantees in correlated setting; experiments reveal performance degradation under model mismatch (Figures 16-17), contradicting theoretical foundation

Overstated 'free of heuristic tuning' claim: requires specification of λ (often unclear), stabilization period duration, debounce window, and moving average window (empirically set to 20)—these design choices constitute data-driven tuning despite claims of parameter-freeness

Performance degradation under model mismatch and unknown costs: Figures 16-17 show weaker performance on NATS cifar100/ImageNet; Figure 19 (unknown costs) doesn't consistently beat simple heuristics (GSS, Convergence), limiting practical applicability
Limited novelty: extends existing theory (Pandora's Box) to stopping rather than proposing new acquisition functions; extension to correlated BO is heuristic without optimality guarantees

strengths: Addresses an important but underexplored practical problem: cost-aware stopping in Bayesian optimization with varying evaluation costs
Principled theoretical framework grounded in Pandora's Box theory, with elegant proof that PBGI and LogEIPC stopping rules are equivalent
First formal theoretical guarantee bounding cost-adjusted simple regret for adaptive stopping in correlated Bayesian optimization
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple settings (1D/8D synthetic, LCBench hyperparameter tuning, NATS neural architecture search) with thorough comparisons to baselines
Well-structured and clearly presented paper with intuitive explanations, helpful visualizations, and extensive appendix providing reproducibility details
Thoughtful treatment of practical implementation concerns including unknown costs, cost model mismatch, and model misspecification
Lemma 1 provides intuitive characterization that expected improvement remains ≥ cost before stopping, which distinguishes the approach from other rules
weaknesses: Weak theoretical guarantee: Theorem 2 only shows regret ≤ immediate stopping (trivial baseline), provides no convergence rate or relative improvement over other stopping rules, and relies on model match assumption that rarely holds in practice
Practical improvements are marginal and inconsistent: method performs competitively on ~75% of LCBench datasets but underperforms significantly on ~25%, with limited analysis of failure modes
Requires domain knowledge to set cost conversion parameter λ; paper provides no practical guidance despite claiming λ should be 'set by the problem provider', limiting real-world applicability
Significant sensitivity to model misspecification: substantial performance degradation on NATS datasets (Figures 15-16) when true objective doesn't match GP prior, yet theory assumes model match
Practical implementation requires heuristic fixes (stabilization periods, debouncing) that lack theoretical justification and suggest fragility, undermining the principled nature of the approach

Empirical evaluation uses proxy costs during optimization but actual costs for evaluation, introducing model mismatch by design; unknown-cost results (Figure 18) sometimes underperform trivial immediate-stopping baseline
Core stopping rule is relatively straightforward extension of Weitzman's 1979 rule to correlated settings; connection to LogEIPC follows from algebraic manipulation rather than deep insight

strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored problem with clear real-world motivation (e.g., cloud-based hyperparameter tuning)
Principled theoretical approach grounded in Pandora's Box theory and Gittins indices, providing solid conceptual foundation
First formal guarantee on cost-adjusted simple regret for general (correlated) Bayesian optimization settings (Theorem 2)
Comprehensive experimental validation: 1D/8D synthetic, LCBench, NATS-Bench with multiple cost regimes, ~50 seeds per trial, extensive baselines
Thoughtful treatment of practical deployment challenges: unknown costs via GP modeling, spurious stop prevention, budget-constrained extension
Elegant connection showing PBGI and LogEIPC stopping criteria are equivalent through algebraic transformations
Generally strong empirical performance: ~75% of LCBench datasets competitive; robust across acquisition functions; outperforms several baselines on cost-adjusted regret
weaknesses: Theoretical guarantee is weak: Theorem 2 only bounds regret by U+C (immediate stopping baseline), providing no improvement guarantee over trivial policy
Limited scope of theoretical results: applies only to PBGI/LogEIPC, not to KG/MES; doesn't extend naturally to other acquisition functions; bound lacks problem-dependent convergence rates

Performance inconsistency: ~25% of LCBench datasets show consistent underperformance (Figures 19-21); significant degradation on NATS-Bench under model mismatch (Figures 15-16); underperforms heuristics in unknown-cost setting

Practical method requires multiple tuning choices despite 'principled' framing: λ conversion rate (domain-dependent), stabilization period length, debouncing window size (20 used without justification); these appear as post-hoc additions rather than core design
Model mismatch vulnerability: Empirical results degrade substantially when proxy cost ≠ actual cost; no detection or mitigation strategy provided; theoretical guarantees assume perfect GP model match
Limited novelty: core insight is recognizing Weitzman's (1979) Pandora's Box stopping criterion applies via PBGI/LogEIPC equivalence; algebraic connection (Eqs. 6→9→10) is straightforward
Experimental concerns: SRGap-med χ parameter tuned post-hoc (0.01→0.1); KG comparison omitted due to computational cost; unclear how tight hindsight oracle bound is
Insufficient guidance on applicability: when should practitioners use this vs. simpler methods? No characterization of when method works well vs. poorly; failure on small datasets unexplained
